claims.text: Local chemical ordering governs the strength of multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local chemical ordering governs the deformation or failure behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys.
Fluctuations in local shear-fault energy govern the strength and deformation or failure behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local chemical ordering and local shear-fault-energy fluctuations affect mechanical behavior by influencing the formation and mobility of deformation-induced defects.
The relevant deformation-induced defects include dislocations and stacking faults.
Interactions among local chemical ordering, local shear-fault-energy fluctuations, and deformation-induced defects control alloy mechanical behavior.
Higher local chemical ordering produces higher strength and greater resistance to deformation.
Lower fluctuations in local shear-fault energy produce higher strength and greater resistance to deformation.
Lower local chemical ordering produces lower strength and greater susceptibility to deformation and failure.
Higher fluctuations in local shear-fault energy produce lower strength and greater susceptibility to deformation and failure.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply across variations in temperature, strain rate, and stress state.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for multi-component concentrated alloys with complex compositions and microstructures.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys with simple compositions or microstructures.
The exact relationship among local chemical ordering, local shear-fault-energy fluctuations, and deformation-induced defects is not fully understood.
Absence of a significant correlation between the proposed structural variables and defect behavior, or insensitivity of mechanical behavior to those variables, would falsify the hypothesis.
